title: What is Geography? Maps & Skills
description: An introduction to geography — physical, human and environmental branches — plus the core map skills: grid references, scale, compass directions, symbols and contour lines.

notes.heading: What is Geography?
notes.body: Geography is the study of the Earth's landscapes, environments and people, and the connections between them. The word comes from the Greek 'geo' (Earth) and 'graphia' (to write or describe) — literally, describing the Earth. Geography has three main branches. Physical geography studies natural features and processes: rivers, mountains, coasts, weather, climate and ecosystems. Human geography studies people and how they live: population, migration, cities, farming, industry and trade. Environmental geography links the two — it studies how people and nature interact, including issues like deforestation, pollution and climate change. Geographers ask four key questions about anything they study: What is it? Where is it? Why is it there? How might it change? Geography matters because it helps us understand our world, make better decisions (where to build, how to prepare for floods), and solve problems from local traffic jams to global climate change.

notes.heading: Maps and Atlases
notes.body: A map is a scaled-down, flat representation of part of the Earth's surface. Because maps are drawn to scale, they let us measure real distances and find places accurately. There are many types of map, each with a different purpose. Political maps show countries, borders, capitals and major cities. Physical maps show natural features such as mountains, rivers and deserts, often using colour shading for height. Topographic maps (such as Ordnance Survey maps in the UK) show the land in great detail — height, roads, footpaths, buildings and boundaries — using symbols and contour lines. Thematic maps focus on one type of information, such as rainfall, population density or soil type. Road maps and street maps are designed for navigation and travel. An atlas is a book (or website) of maps covering countries, continents and the whole world, usually with an index so you can look up any place. When using an atlas, always check the scale bar, the key (legend) and the title first — these tell you what the map shows and how to read it.

notes.heading: Grid References: 4-Figure and 6-Figure
notes.body: Ordnance Survey maps are divided into 1 km squares by grid lines. Vertical lines are called eastings (their numbers increase as you go east) and horizontal lines are called northings (numbers increase going north). A 4-figure grid reference identifies a whole 1 km square. Read the easting number first, then the northing — remember 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'. The reference gives the numbers of the lines that meet at the bottom-left (south-west) corner of the square. A 6-figure grid reference pinpoints a smaller square, one tenth of a grid square in each direction (100 m × 100 m). First find the 4-figure square, then mentally divide it into tenths: the third digit is the number of tenths east, and the sixth digit is the number of tenths north. For example, in reference 326451: 32 is the easting line, 6 means six-tenths further east, 45 is the northing line, and 1 means one-tenth further north. Worked example: a church stands in the square whose bottom-left corner is where easting 28 meets northing 74, six-tenths east and three-tenths north — its 6-figure reference is 286743.

notes.heading: Scale and Measuring Distance
notes.body: Scale tells you how much the real world has been shrunk to fit on the map. It can be written in three ways. A ratio (representative fraction) such as 1:25 000 means 1 unit on the map equals 25 000 of the same units on the ground — so 1 cm on the map = 25 000 cm = 250 m in reality, and 4 cm on the map = 1 km. A linear (graphic) scale is a printed bar marked with real distances (km or miles) that you measure against. A word statement simply says '1 cm to 1 km'. Ordnance Survey Explorer maps use 1:25 000 (4 cm = 1 km) and Landranger maps use 1:50 000 (2 cm = 1 km). To measure a straight-line distance, measure between the two points with a ruler and convert using the scale. To measure a winding route such as a road or river, lay a piece of string or a strip of paper along it, marking the corners, then straighten it out and measure the total length. Worked example: on a 1:50 000 map, two villages are 8 cm apart in a straight line. Real distance = 8 × 50 000 cm = 400 000 cm = 4 km.

notes.heading: Compass Directions
notes.body: Compass directions describe where places are in relation to each other. The four cardinal points are North (N), East (E), South (S) and West (W). Between them lie the four ordinal (intercardinal) points: North-East (NE), South-East (SE), South-West (SW) and North-West (NW). Together these make the eight points of the compass. A 16-point compass adds further divisions such as North-North-East (NNE) and East-North-East (ENE). Directions can also be given as bearings — angles measured clockwise from North, written with three figures. North = 000°, East = 090°, South = 180°, West = 270°, North-East = 045°. To give a direction between two places on a map, imagine standing at the starting point facing North, then turn towards the destination. A useful memory aid for the order N, E, S, W is 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat'. Remember: compass points are always read clockwise, starting from North at the top of a map unless a north arrow shows otherwise.

notes.heading: Map Symbols and the Key
notes.body: Maps use symbols to show features clearly without words. Because every feature on a map is shown by a symbol, you must use the key (legend) — the panel that explains what each symbol means — to read the map properly. Ordnance Survey symbols fall into three types. Point symbols mark something at one spot: a small black square for a building, a cross for a church with a tower, a dot with a triangle for a campsite, or a blue 'P' for parking. Line symbols show linear features: black lines for railways (with station symbols), coloured bands for roads (blue for motorways, red for main A roads, orange for secondary roads, yellow or unfilled for minor roads), dashed lines for footpaths and bridleways, and thin blue lines for rivers. Area symbols shade or pattern whole zones: green shading for woodland, blue for water, and special letters for features like nature reserves. Many symbols look like tiny pictures of what they represent — a triangle for a hill, a picnic table for a picnic site — which makes them easier to learn. Always check which OS map series your key belongs to, because symbols can differ slightly between 1:25 000 and 1:50 000 maps.

notes.heading: Contour Lines and Height
notes.body: Maps need to show not just where things are, but how high the land is. A contour line joins points of equal height above sea level. On OS maps, contours are thin orange-brown lines, usually drawn every 5 or 10 metres of height, with the height in metres sometimes printed along the line. The pattern of contours tells you the shape of the land. Contours close together mean a steep slope; contours far apart mean a gentle slope; no contours at all mean flat land. Closed loops of contours show a hill or mountain, with height increasing towards the centre. A V-shape in the contours pointing uphill (up-valley) marks a valley; contours jutting downhill mark a spur or ridge. Height is also shown in other ways: spot heights are a dot with a number giving the exact height of a point in metres; triangulation pillars (trig points) are marked with a small triangle and a height; and layer colouring (colour shading between height bands, green low down through brown to white for the highest peaks) is common on atlas and physical maps. Reading contours lets you picture the landscape in three dimensions from a flat map — a key skill for walkers, engineers and planners.

flashcards.definition: The branch of geography that studies natural features and processes of the Earth, such as rivers, mountains, weather and ecosystems.
flashcards.example: Studying how a waterfall forms, or how a glacier shapes a valley.

flashcards.definition: The branch of geography that studies people and their activities — population, migration, settlements, farming and industry.
flashcards.example: Investigating why a city's population is growing rapidly.

flashcards.definition: The branch linking physical and human geography, studying how people and the natural environment affect each other.
flashcards.example: Analysing how farming practices cause soil erosion.

flashcards.definition: The vertical grid lines on an OS map; their numbers increase as you travel east. Read first in any grid reference.
flashcards.example: In the 4-figure reference 2874, '28' is the easting.

flashcards.definition: The horizontal grid lines on an OS map; their numbers increase as you travel north. Read second in any grid reference.
flashcards.example: In the 4-figure reference 2874, '74' is the northing.

flashcards.definition: A reference that pinpoints a location within a 100 m × 100 m area by dividing a 1 km grid square into tenths.
flashcards.example: A church at 286743 is six-tenths east and three-tenths north inside square 2874.

flashcards.definition: The relationship between distance on a map and distance on the ground, shown as a ratio, a linear scale bar or a word statement.
flashcards.example: On a 1:25 000 map, 1 cm on the map represents 250 m on the ground.

flashcards.definition: The four main compass directions: North, East, South and West.
A direction given as a three-figure angle measured clockwise from North (000°).
flashcards.example: East is a bearing of 090°; South-West is 225°.

flashcards.definition: The panel on a map that explains what every symbol, colour and line means.
flashcards.example: Checking the key to learn that a dashed black line means a footpath.

flashcards.definition: A line on a map joining points of equal height above sea level, used to show the shape and steepness of the land.
flashcards.example: Contours packed close together on a map warn walkers of a steep slope.

flashcards.definition: A dot on a map with a number giving the exact height above sea level at that single point, in metres.
flashcards.example: A dot marked '352' on a hilltop means the summit is 352 m above sea level.

questions.stem: Which branch of geography studies natural features such as rivers, mountains and weather?
choices: Human geography
Physical geography
Economic geography
Historical geography
questions.explanation: Physical geography is the study of natural features and processes. Human geography studies people and their activities, so the river itself is physical — although how people use the river would be human geography.

questions.stem: On an OS map, what are 'eastings'?
choices: Horizontal grid lines whose numbers increase northwards
Vertical grid lines whose numbers increase eastwards
Symbols showing buildings
Lines joining points of equal height
questions.explanation: Eastings are the vertical grid lines, numbered so values increase as you go east. Horizontal lines increasing northwards are northings, and lines of equal height are contours.

questions.stem: What does a 4-figure grid reference identify?
choices: An exact point on the map
A 1 km grid square
A 100 m square
The height of a hill
questions.explanation: A 4-figure grid reference gives the easting and northing lines that meet at the bottom-left corner of a 1 km square, so it identifies that whole square — you need 6 figures to narrow down to 100 m.

questions.stem: A map has a scale of 1:50 000. How far apart on the ground are two places that are 6 cm apart on the map?
choices: 1.2 km
3 km
12 km
questions.explanation: 6 cm × 50 000 = 300 000 cm. Dividing by 100 000 (cm per km) gives 3 km. On a 1:50 000 map, 2 cm equals 1 km, so 6 cm equals 3 km.

questions.stem: Which is the correct rule for giving any grid reference?
choices: Read the northing first, then the easting
Read the easting first, then the northing ('along the corridor, then up the stairs')
Always start from the top-right corner of the square
Read whichever number is larger first
questions.explanation: Grid references always give the easting (along the bottom) before the northing (up the side). Reversing them points to a completely different square.

questions.stem: A campsite is in grid square 3367, four-tenths of the way east and nine-tenths of the way north across the square. What is its 6-figure grid reference?
questions.explanation: Start with the 4-figure square 3367. Insert the tenths: easting 33 + 4 tenths gives 334; northing 67 + 9 tenths gives 679. The full reference is 334679.

questions.stem: What is the compass direction exactly halfway between North and East?
choices: North-West
South-East
North-East
East-North-East
questions.explanation: The ordinal point between North and East is North-East (NE). North-West lies between North and West, and East-North-East is a 16-point direction just north of East.

questions.stem: On a bearing measured clockwise from North, which direction is 270°?
choices: East
South
West
North-West
questions.explanation: Bearings run clockwise from North = 000°: East = 090°, South = 180°, West = 270°. So 270° is due west.

questions.stem: Why must you always consult the key (legend) before reading an unfamiliar map?
choices: The key shows the map's copyright date
The key explains what each symbol and colour on the map means
The key lists the names of all streets
The key tells you which direction is north
questions.explanation: Maps communicate through symbols rather than words, and symbols can vary between map series. The key is the only reliable guide to what each symbol, line and colour represents.

questions.stem: On an OS map, contours are packed very close together down one side of a hill and far apart on the other. What does this tell you?
choices: The close-contour side is a gentle slope and the far-apart side is steep
The close-contour side is steep and the far-apart side is gentle
The hill is higher on the side with more contours
Both sides are equally steep
questions.explanation: Close contours mean height changes quickly over a short horizontal distance — a steep slope. Widely spaced contours mean height changes slowly — a gentle slope.

questions.stem: A walker wants to measure the length of a winding footpath on a 1:25 000 map. What is the best method?
choices: Measure the straight-line distance with a ruler and multiply by 25 000
Count the number of grid squares the path crosses
Lay string along the path, straighten it, measure its length and convert using the scale
Estimate it from the contour pattern alone
questions.explanation: A ruler only measures straight lines, so it badly underestimates a winding route. Laying string (or a paper strip) along the path and then measuring it straight captures every bend before converting with the scale.

questions.stem: Two maps cover the same area. Map A is 1:25 000 and Map B is 1:50 000. Which statement is correct?
choices: Map B shows more detail because its scale number is bigger
Map A shows more detail and 4 cm on it equals 1 km on the ground
Both maps show identical detail
Map A shows less detail because 1 cm represents a shorter distance
questions.explanation: A 1:25 000 map is a larger scale — each centimetre represents only 250 m, so features are drawn bigger and in more detail. On it 4 cm = 1 km, whereas 2 cm = 1 km on a 1:50 000 map.

questions.stem: You stand at a spot height marked 214 m. The next contour line you cross heading uphill is labelled 220 m. On a map with 10 m contour intervals, what is the height of the previous contour you crossed?
questions.explanation: With 10 m intervals the contour below 220 m is 210 m. The spot height of 214 m sits between the 210 m and 220 m contours, which is consistent.

questions.stem: A 6-figure grid reference ends in the digits ...4 ...5 (e.g. 124565). Where within its 1 km grid square is the location?
choices: At the bottom-left corner of the square
Near the centre of the square
At the top-right corner of the square
On the eastern edge of the square
questions.explanation: A third digit of 4 and a sixth digit of 5 place the point about halfway across (east) and halfway up (north) the grid square — close to its centre.

questions.stem: A valley crosses a hillside on an OS map. Which contour pattern correctly shows the valley?
choices: Contours form V-shapes pointing uphill, towards higher land
Contours form V-shapes pointing downhill, towards lower land
Contours form perfect circles
Contours stop completely at the valley floor
questions.explanation: Where a stream cuts a valley, each contour bends into a V that points uphill (up-valley, towards higher ground). Contours that jut downhill form a spur or ridge instead — the classic 'V points up the valley' rule.
